story_text.value:
I built Sidelong because I wanted one single place to store, search, and summarize all the stuff I was reading, watching, and listening to.

Save any link, article, podcast, youtube video, local file, or a bunch of other content types. Sidelong presents and embed the content, summarizes the top insights. You can subscribe to newsletters and get them sent and ingested directly, and follow your favorite podcasts and youtube channels to have the new episodes ready for you automatically. Highlight or take notes on what was interesting in anything above right in the app.

Sidelong takes what you learn, and gives you a daily summary that connects dots across the sources you saved. It also learns about your interests and recommends what you might want to check out next.

If you ever wanted to write about the stuff you're learning, you can use the built in editor which connects what you are writing with all the things you saved and presents it to you while you right.

Alot of other features like MCP, AI chat, etc as well.

story_text.value:
In 2024, multiple Nobel Prizes were awarded for AI related accomplishments:

> 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics: Awarded to John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for foundational discoveries and inventions enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks.

(Source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton)

> 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry: Awarded to Demis Hassabis and John M. Jumper for developing an AI algorithm (AlphaFold) that predicts complex three-dimensional protein structures

(Source https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02527-z)

I would classify the work that got them the physics prize as basic research that played a big part in enabling AI. And the prize in Chemistry falls into a similar category I think…

Now, both openAI + Anthropic are maybe less involved in basic research directly but the things they "produce" are now used to solve problems humanity tried to solve for many many years. If they both published all of their papers under a different name, a name that sounds like a real persons name, I am sure that person would be considered for multiple Nobel Prizes.

It rarely happens but "organizations" can receive Nobel Prizes. Eg.:

> The European Union (EU) won the 2012 Nobel Peace Prize for over six decades of advancing peace, reconciliation, democracy, and human rights in Europe

So why not OpenAI + Anthropic? (Yes, its maybe still a bit early, given that some of the papers still are pending proper peer review - but overall the question remains: How would humanity deal with "that"? "That" being that the "products" of two companies made those scientific breakthroughs?

title.value: Ask HN: Nobel Prizes for OpenAI and Anthropic: When?

story_text.value:
Hi friends, genuine question.

We all see that top notch Mathematicians can use LLM to prove world class results in a relatively short time of period. OK I admit some of the results are not verified yet, but please hear me. Neither do I know how much “brain” is human and how much is the LLM, because we don’t see the prompts.

My question is: what do you think about your career in the future?

Please hear me out. In the current world, the way you become a Mathematician, is to get good scores, go to schools, take PHD and then professorship. There may be middle steps like postdoctoral or industry experience, but that’s the general way to do it.

And the way that schools judge professors, if I understand correctly, is more about how much results you can get —- ofc if you can obtain big grants then the better, but most of you can’t do that, so I assume that it’s more about the papers. You also teach but that’s not as big as the research. For now, there are a lot of smaller problems left to solve, and since world class Mathematicians tend to devote their life to one world class problem, there are plenty of food for everyone.

Does the above make sense? This leads me to the question of: if the future of getting proofs is to prompt with an LLM or whatever AI solution, and it is apparent that world class Mathematicians can prove more conjectures or whatever than they ever can dream without LLM, why do schools need mediocre Mathematicians? I’m not trying to belittle you, but I’m trying to figure out career paths for my son, and I need to understand the impact of AI to all career paths.

Again, I iterate, if one world class Mathematicians can prompt through many problems in their lifetime, we face two possibilities:

1. LLMs are good at solving problems but not good at asking new questions, so eventually we have few questions to crack, so the world doesn’t really need that many Mathematicians.

2. LLM is equally good at asking new questions. Well again I don’t see why the school needs to hire so many Mathematicians.

Again, I believe LLM is merely the tool here, you still need the Mathematicians to do the thinking —- this does NOT contradict what I wrote.

Of course, there is another part of your work, that is to teach Mathematics. But I’m not sure that is unique to humans. Maybe LLM can do that too. It just needs more training on that because so far the training is more on proving things, not teaching things.

I want to iterate a third time, that I’m not belittling you. You are smarter than me, so please help me understand the situation. This is more about employment, not about interests —- if one is interested in Math, sure go ahead and learn the hell out of it —- but persuading people to pay you to do that is different.

Thanks in advance.

title.value: Ask HN: For professional Mathematicians –- about your career in the future

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Fengli, founder of Inxpanse. HeyCube is our first product: the personalized feed for your always-on AI agents.

While building my own always-on agents, I kept watching the token and search API costs add up really fast. Then I noticed the scheduled tasks in ChatGPT/Grok Bot/etc. also use up a lot of your plan's allowance, often on checks that find nothing new. That's why many people still don't leave their agents truly always on.

This reminded me of the eras we humans have been through too: first search engines, then feeds. So I thought, why not build agents a feed of their own? That's why we built HeyCube. It reads sources around the clock and sends what fits you to the right agent, so your tokens go to the work itself. It's free and live at heycube.ai now, and works with ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Muse, Claude Code, and other agents in beta.

I'm looking forward to you giving your agents a feed and seeing what they can do. Let me know if you have any questions/comments/feature requests :) Thanks!

story_text.value:
Hello HN,

It's been a rough couple of days and weeks on the tech world + tech stock markets, so to unwind a little bit I created this fun game that presents 5 headlines every day and you need to pick your confidence on whether it's Real or it's a "Bubble".

Note that I don't want to make a judgment call on whether we are indeed in an AI bubble or not, and whether it's collapsing or not. The name and the game goes both ways and could support both cases imo. And the whole point of the game is exactly to try getting out of the whole speculation and have a little of fun.

There is no back-end, no auth, no account. It's just a JS bundle updated daily for the new questions to pop up. Your daily stats are stored in localStorage so if you want to keep your stats you need to use the same device evey day.

Cheers, Guilherme Perotta

story_text.value:
Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS:

Repo: https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics/dualayer-hierarchy-stand... Full Specification (23-page PDF): https://zainiumdynamics.tech/dhs

DHS 1.1 defines a layered filesystem hierarchy for immutable Linux systems where musl and glibc coexist side by side without conflict. Either C library can be primary; the distribution chooses.

Root layout (no /usr, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /lib64, /etc, /var, or /boot at /, not even as symlinks):

  /
  |-- overlayer/   (the entire OS: all layers)
  |-- home/        (user home directories)
  |-- root/        (root home)
  |-- dev/         (devtmpfs)
  |-- proc/        (procfs)
  |-- sys/         (sysfs)
  |-- run/         (tmpfs; removable media at /run/media/user/label)
  `-- tmp/         (temporary files)
Layer structure under /overlayer (composed at boot via OverlayFS with syshub as lower and userland/union as upper):

  /overlayer/
  |-- syshub/           (read-only base OS; boots without userland)
  |-- userland/         (installed packages: union/, work/, registry/)
  |-- ignition/         (kernels, initramfs, bootloader; read-only)
  |-- agents/           (optional AI coding agent instructions/policies)
  `-- .syshub-pending/  (staged atomic base upgrade, applied at next boot)
Dual-libc isolation: musl and glibc each live in their own GNU target-triplet directory (arch-vendor-linux-musl and arch-vendor-linux-gnu) with separate loaders, headers, C++ runtimes, loader configs, and toolchains. Shared directories (/overlayer/syshub/bin, lib, include) belong strictly to the primary libc and search paths never cross, while both read shared system config (passwd, hosts, resolv.conf, zoneinfo) from /overlayer/syshub/etc.

FHS compatibility: Foreign packages are adapted at install time (PT_INTERP, RPATH, pkg-config, shebangs). Runtime FHS path lookups use a preload resolver and loader redirection (the known LD_PRELOAD limitation for static/setuid binaries is documented in Chapter 7).

Reference implementation — Zainium OS (https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics): - Layers: syshub (base), zexlib (userland), zaisys (ignition) - Libc design: Design A (musl primary in base, glibc as a userland package) - Boot & atomic upgrades: quantra-ramfs - Package manager & receipts: zex - Path/loader resolver & toolchain switcher: libsys_resolver.so, sys-resolver - Protected base/ignition paths: elevate, elevate-pam

Looking for honest technical critique on where this layout holds up, where it breaks down, and what edge cases are missing.

Dual-libc isolation: musl and glibc each live in their own GNU target-triplet directory (arch-vendor-linux-musl and arch-vendor-linux-gnu) with separate loaders, headers, C++ runtimes, loader configs, and toolchains. Shared directories (/overlayer/syshub/bin, lib, include) belong strictly to the primary libc and search paths never cross, while both read shared system config (passwd, hosts, resolv.conf, zoneinfo) from /overlayer/syshub/etc.

FHS compatibility: Foreign packages are adapted at install time (PT_INTERP, RPATH, pkg-config, shebangs). Runtime FHS path lookups use a preload resolver and loader redirection (the known LD_PRELOAD limitation for static/setuid binaries is documented in Chapter 7).

Reference implementation — Zainium OS (https://github.com/Zainium-Dynamics): - Layers: syshub (base), zexlib (userland), zaisys (ignition) - Libc design: Design A (musl primary in base, glibc as a userland package) - Boot & atomic upgrades: quantra-ramfs - Package manager & receipts: zex - Path/loader resolver & toolchain switcher: libsys_resolver.so, sys-resolver - Protected base/ignition paths: elevate, elevate-pam

Looking for honest technical critique on where this layout holds up, where it breaks down, and what edge cases are missing.

fmgrep is a (Claude-powered) open source reimplementation of a FAANG code search engine I was involved in a few years back. It's aimed at very large (e.g. AOSP) source trees.

Instead of n-grams,`fmgrep` builds an FM index of the tree with O(pattern) `count` and O(occurrences) `locate`, which is quite cool and leads to blazing fast performance as seen in the benchmarks.

story_text.value:
Pintura is designed for AI agents to work on plaintext files and for humans to review in a browser.

The premise is that when you're doing slides with AI agents, you mainly need to review their work and iterate until you're happy.

The main benefits are: 1. You can use git for version control and clear diffs. 2. The browser UI is designed for review: flip between versions with visual changes highlighted, pin comments, or drag/reword directly. 3. Your agent gets a CLI that helps it catch things like text overflow, misaligned elements, hanging words, etc.

It pairs with our spreadsheet companion Libreta (github.com/editide/libreta) if you want to link numbers. Clicking a linked number on a slide pops up a spreadsheet showing the formula or a screenshot of the original source.

I've been using this to build financial decks from the terminal with Claude Code (and now Antigravity). It's much nicer than flipping back and forth between Excel and PowerPoint. Here are some decks I've built with this setup: https://iterativaresearch.com/

Everything (preview, checks, screenshots, HTML/PDF export) is Apache-2.0 and runs locally with no account. PowerPoint export currently runs through our API with a free plan.

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Raymond, a long-time reader of the site.

For the past year I've been working on Animama, a free and open-source (AGPL) AI desktop companion with 3D anime-style avatars.

A quick rundown of the Anima (AI companion) features:

- Personality: an IDENTITY.md file you can edit

- Memories: a memory filesystem of Markdown files. Animas have tools to read and write these files, and you can edit them too

- Emotions: Animas can express 24 emotions, which drive their facial expressions, tone of voice and behavior

- Behavior: 300+ gestures and reactions, built on a custom JSON animation format (animaPoseClip)

- Structured output: every reply is text plus an emotion and a gesture, which the avatar acts out as it speaks

You bring your own API key. The low-cost models from OpenAI (GPT-6 Luna) and Anthropic (Claude Haiku 5.5) are good enough, so a few dollars of usage goes a long way. Local models are supported but still experimental.

When I started, pretty much all human-AI interaction was typing into a chat box and getting a wall of text back. I felt this could be made more engaging, interactive and fun. Like everything else in AI, things have improved a lot since then. We now have speech-to-speech models (GPT Live, Gemini Realtime), and even the frontier labs have released their own AI avatars (Codex pets, Grok's Ani). Animama is just one solo developer's take on it.

My original idea was an AI productivity companion (think Clippy, RIP), and it still kind of is. But it's obviously never going to compete with the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps, so I leaned more into the character side of things.

Anyways, I built this because I thought it would be a fun project. But, it did make me realize that there are some serious risks to AI Companion apps, so I've made the app 18+ with safety guardrails built in (e.g. an Anima admits it's an AI if you sincerely ask).

Three ways to try it:

1. Desktop app (Apple silicon Mac, Windows 11, linux and windows 10 coming soon): https://animama.ai/download

2. Self-host with Docker: see the README

3. Web demo: sign up at https://animama.ai

Docs: https://docs.animama.ai

Happy to answer any questions!

story_text.value:
In 2020, I wrote Rocketcrab, a lobby service and launcher for mobile web party games. (Hacker News post from 2020: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24876148)

You would create a "party," which gave you a URL like rocketcrab.com/abcd that you could send to your friends. You could choose from a library of games, and those games would be shown on everyone's devices via iframe.

The site was fairly successful, probably mostly because I forced all the users of my game Drawphone (https://rocketcrab.com/game/drawphone) to play it via Rocketcrab. ;D But over the years, I lost interest in maintaining Rocketcrab. People are still playing, though, so I kept paying the $12/month for the server!

Recently, with the new AI coding agents, I was inspired to bring two ideas to life in Rocketcrab: make-your-own vibe-coded games and serverless multiplayer.

The vibe-coded games feature is called Nova: you copy a prompt into your favorite AI, work with it to build a game, and paste the resulting one-shot HTML back into Rocketcrab. No login needed! The HTML is stored only in your browser and is sent to your friends via iframe when playing together.

For serverless multiplayer, I used the awesome open-source P2P library Trystero (https://trystero.dev/), with some Cloudflare Durable Objects and fallback TURN for strict enterprise networks.

Rocketcrab is 100% free and open-source under the MIT license. The rewrite was done mostly with Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.2 Sol, plus a security audit with Gemini 4 Neon.

Feel free to send me any ideas or feedback, or open issues and pull requests on GitHub: https://github.com/tannerkrewson/rocketcrab

I just cut over to the rewrite a few hours ago, so let me know if there are any issues! I'm planning to add some new games I've found on the web to the library, just as soon as my five-hour Claude window resets. :D

PS: You've got about a day left to build a Nova game and try it with your family tomorrow... happy thanksgiving!
